question: A team configures 2 shared + 64 routed quarter-size experts and routes to 8 routed experts, keeping the same 2 shared. Compared with DeepSeekMoE 16B (2 + 6 active), what changed?
options: Nothing; shared experts do not count toward compute
Total parameters rose by 2 experts
Activated expert compute rose from 8 to 10 quarter-experts, i.e. from 2 to 2.5 standard FFNs per token
Only the router cost changed
explain: Shared experts always run, so they count fully toward activated compute. DeepSeekMoE lowers the routed top-K by $K_s$ to keep compute fixed: 2 + 6 = 8 quarter-size experts = 2 FFNs. Using 2 + 8 means 10 quarters = 2.5 FFNs, 25% more expert FLOPs.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: MoE on real hardware: expert parallelism, all-to-all and serving
question: A team switches from 64 experts with top-2 to 256 experts with top-8, each a quarter as wide, keeping active parameters fixed. A step routes 2048 tokens. How many rows does each expert's GEMM get on average, and what changes?
options: 16 rows after the switch, because 4 times as many experts share the tokens
256 rows after the switch, because top-8 sends 4 times as many copies of each token
Nothing changes, because FLOPs per token are equal
64 rows in both designs (2048 x 2 / 64 and 2048 x 8 / 256), so intensity stays near 60, but there are 4 times as many GEMMs, each a quarter the size, and each token goes to 4 times as many experts
explain: Tokens per expert = B x K / N, and K and N both grew 4 times. Rows per expert stay at 64, so each GEMM is still memory-bound at the same intensity, but the same work is now split over 4 times as many smaller launches and dispatch destinations. Fine granularity costs efficiency unless kernels group the experts and batches grow.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Secure Boot keys: PK, KEK, db and dbx
question: A laptop has no PK enrolled. What does the UEFI spec say about writing db?
options: It is impossible
It can be written without a signature check, because the platform is in setup mode
It needs Microsoft's signature
Only the TPM can write it
explain: With no PK the platform is in setup mode, and the signature databases can be written without signature validation. That is why a missing PK is a finding in its own right.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Measured boot: PCRs, extend and what each PCR records
question: Secure Boot is switched off in the setup menu, and nothing else changes. Which PCR is designed to reveal this?
options: PCR0
PCR4
PCR7
PCR12
explain: PFP 1.06 requires the SecureBoot variable and the PK, KEK, db and dbx contents to be measured into PCR7, the Secure Boot policy PCR.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: Case: LogoFAIL, a boot logo parsed by the most trusted code
question: Why did Secure Boot not stop LogoFAIL?
options: Secure Boot was disabled on all affected devices
Secure Boot verifies executables before running them; a logo is data parsed by already-trusted firmware code
The logos were signed by Microsoft
Secure Boot only runs after the OS starts
explain: The vulnerable code is the trusted firmware itself. Feeding it malicious data needs no unsigned executable, so nothing for Secure Boot to reject.

courseTitle: Firmware and boot security: UEFI, Secure Boot and bootkits
lessonTitle: A defender's firmware playbook, and where to practise
question: Which piece of evidence is hardest for malware already running in the OS kernel to forge?
options: A health report from the local EDR agent
A TPM quote over PCRs with the verifier's fresh nonce, checked against a replayed event log
The Windows event log
A screenshot of the setup menu
explain: The kernel can tamper with agents and logs. It cannot produce a TPM signature over PCR values it cannot reset, bound to a nonce it did not choose.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-3 inside a warpgroup, and FP8 done accurately
question: Your FA3-style kernel (head dimension 128, consumers at 240 registers) spills after you enlarge the key block size $B_c$ from 176 to 256. Which part of the 2-stage pipeline is most directly to blame?
options: The extra $S_{next}$ buffer of $B_r \times B_c$ FP32 values kept in registers
The TMA descriptors, which grow with $B_c$
The circular SMEM buffer, which lives in registers
The log-sum-exp vector, which grows with $B_c$
explain: The paper calls out exactly this tradeoff: the 2-stage pipeline holds an extra $S_{next}$ of size $B_r \times B_c \times$ sizeof(float) per thread block, which competes with larger block sizes. SMEM buffers are not in registers, and the log-sum-exp has one value per query row ($B_r$), not per key.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Why LLM serving needs its own attention engine
question: A decode step for Llama-style GQA with 32 query heads and 8 KV heads. Ignoring other effects, how much does GQA raise attention's operational intensity over plain multi-head attention with the same query count?
options: About 4x, because each KV head serves $g = 4$ query heads
Not at all, decode is always $O(1)$
About 32x, one per query head
It depends only on the page size
explain: The group size is $g = H_{qo}/H_{kv} = 32/8 = 4$. Each key and value loaded from HBM is reused by 4 query heads, so intensity becomes $O(g \cdot l_{qo}) = O(4)$. Page size changes how KV is addressed, not how often each byte is reused.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode in one launch: POD and persistent batches
question: In which batch does fusing prefill and decode attention into one launch help MOST, by the roofline model?
options: 64 decodes of 4K tokens and no prefill
One 8K-token prefill chunk at position 32K and 64 decodes of 1K tokens
A prefill chunk needing about 300 us of math alongside decodes needing about 300 us of KV reads
Any batch, because one launch always halves the time
explain: Overlap saves at most the smaller of the two kernels' bottleneck times, so it pays most when they are similar: about 1.85x in the lesson's model. A decode-only batch has nothing to hide. A huge prefill dwarfs the decodes (5.0 ms of math against 0.08 ms of reads), so the gain is about 2%. One launch can never beat the larger total of compute or memory.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
question: A flow model gives sharp images at 50 Euler steps but blurry, averaged-looking images at 1 step. Which change most directly attacks the cause?
options: Train longer with the same objective
Use a larger batch size
Make the learned paths straighter, for example with reflow or an OT-based coupling
Lower the learning rate at the end of training
explain: A single step follows the initial velocity, which points toward the data mean wherever paths are curved. Training the same objective better converges to the same curved field; straightening the paths is what lets few steps work.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: Three messages, seventeen years: Lowe's attack on Needham-Schroeder
question: Why does adding B inside message 2 stop the attack?
options: It makes message 2 longer, so it cannot be forwarded
It adds a second nonce
A, expecting a reply from I, sees B's name inside the ciphertext and aborts
It lets B detect that I is lying
explain: In the attack, A is running with I and receives a message 2 that B created. With the responder's name inside the encryption, A sees B where it expected I. The intruder cannot change the name because it cannot open or rebuild a ciphertext under A's key with B's nonce inside.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: ProVerif: protocols as processes, proofs by Horn clauses
question: Why does the deterministic ballot fail equivalence even though the intruder can never decrypt it?
options: The intruder can compute aenc(yes, pk) itself from public values and compare it with the ballot
ProVerif assumes the private key leaks
Deterministic encryption is decryptable without the key in the symbolic model
Because yes and no have different lengths
explain: Public-key encryption without randomness lets anyone test a guess: encrypt each candidate plaintext and compare. With a small set of possible messages (yes or no) that reveals the vote. Real public-key encryption is randomized for exactly this reason.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: 5G AKA, Signal and MLS: analyses that changed standards
question: The PQXDH analysis found flaws in the specification that were not exploitable in the Signal app. What is the right reading?
options: The flaws did not matter
Signal's implementation was formally verified end to end
The specification allowed insecure implementations; Signal's implementation choices happened to avoid them, and the spec was updated so other implementers would too
The flaws were in Kyber
explain: Other implementers follow the specification, not Signal's code. The authors worked with the designers to update the specification, verifying each change, so the guarantee no longer depends on one implementation's choices.

courseTitle: Formal methods for security: protocol proofs and verified systems
lessonTitle: Automated reasoning at cloud scale: Zelkova, s2n and Cedar
question: How did Cedar's team check that the production Rust matches the Lean model they proved properties about?
options: They proved the Rust code correct line by line in Lean
Differential random testing: run the model and the Rust on the same random inputs and compare results
Code review only
They compiled Lean to Rust
explain: Proofs cover the model; differential random testing connects the model to the production code, and property-based testing covers unmodelled parts. Together these found 21 bugs beyond the 4 found by proofs.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: TLA+ basics: a system is states plus allowed steps
question: You fix the race by making the increment one atomic step (and remove tmp from the spec): `Inc(p) == pc[p] = "inc" /\ x' = x + 1 /\ pc' = [pc EXCEPT ![p] = "done"]`. What does TLC report for N = 2?
options: Still a violation, because two processes can run Inc in the same step
No error: every step increments x by 1, so x = 2 once both are done
A deadlock error, because Inc can never be enabled
It cannot check it, since x' = x + 1 is an assignment
explain: Next allows exactly one process to take one step at a time, so nothing interleaves inside Inc. TLC confirms it: 4 distinct states, no error (8 states for N = 3). In PlusCal the fix is to put the read and write under one label.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Refinement: proving a detailed design implements an abstract one
question: In TwoPhase, the TM receives a Prepared message, which changes only tmPrepared. What does TCommit see under the refinement mapping?
options: A Prepare step by that RM
A stuttering step, because rmState is unchanged
A violation, since TCommit has no TM
Nothing: refinement checking skips steps that change hidden variables
explain: The mapping exposes only rmState. A step that leaves rmState unchanged maps to a stuttering step, which every TLA+ spec allows. TLC does not skip it; it checks that it is a stutter.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Connecting specs to running code, and the wider tool map
question: A small Rust function parses a length-prefixed packet using unsafe pointer arithmetic, with inputs up to 64 bytes. You want a counterexample if any input can cause out-of-bounds access, with minimal annotation. Which fits best?
options: TLA+ with TLC
P
TLAPS
Kani with a harness over any 64-byte input
explain: This is a code-level, bounded question about one function: exactly what Kani's harnesses and kani::any() are for, and Kani checks for undefined behavior in unsafe code. TLA+, P and TLAPS work on design models, not on the Rust code.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: FP8 beyond the GEMM: communication, optimizer state, memory, speed
question: A team turns on FP8 GEMMs for every linear layer and expects peak memory to halve. It barely changes. Why?
options: FP8 tensors are padded to 16 bits in memory
Most memory is master weights, gradients, optimizer moments and activations that FP8 GEMM inputs do not touch
The amax history uses more memory than the weights
Tensor cores cannot read FP8 from memory
explain: FP8 GEMMs change compute, not the 12 to 16 bytes per parameter of training state. FP8-LM cut memory by moving the gradient and first moment to FP8 and the master weight and second moment to FP16, and DeepSeek-V3 caches activations in FP8.

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Pretraining in NVFP4: the four-part recipe and its results
question: Why does the recipe use 16x16 2D blocks for weights but 1x16 blocks for activations and gradients?
options: 2D blocks are faster for every tensor
Activations cannot be transposed
1x16 blocks are required by E4M3
Weights are reused in both Fprop and Dgrad (transposed), so a scale shared over a square block keeps the two quantized copies identical; activations and gradients benefit more from finer 1x16 scaling
explain: The chain-rule mismatch matters most for weights, and weights can adapt to coarser scaling during training. The report found training less sensitive to inconsistency in activations, so they keep the more accurate 1x16 blocks.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Scraping and enumeration: Facebook's 530 million phone numbers
question: Your app's 'find friends by email' endpoint returns full profiles for matches and has a 10,000 per hour limit per IP address. What is the most important change?
options: Raise the per-IP limit so real users are not blocked
Hash the email addresses before uploading
Switch the response to XML
Cap lookups per account, return only a suggestion, and honour a discoverability setting
explain: Per-IP limits fall to proxies, and hashing emails does not stop matching (the server still answers per identifier). The structural fixes limit volume per identity, minimise what a match reveals, and let users opt out of being found.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: CAPTCHAs, their limits and privacy-preserving tokens
question: At USD 1 per thousand solves, how much does a CAPTCHA on every attempt add to a 100,000-attempt campaign?
options: USD 1
USD 100
USD 10
explain: 100,000 / 1,000 x USD 1 = USD 100. Compare that with the campaign's revenue (lesson 2): a challenge alone often only trims profit.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card payments from zero: who is who, and where fraud lands
question: A developer proposes 'block any card number that fails the Luhn check, and treat Luhn-valid numbers as low risk'. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, Luhn proves the card exists
Luhn only detects typos; a valid check digit says nothing about whether the card is real, funded or the user's own
Luhn is only for debit cards
Luhn checks are illegal under PCI DSS
explain: The check digit is public arithmetic designed to catch typing errors. Rejecting failures early is fine for usability, but passing it carries no risk information.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Measuring it: precision, recall, friction and the missing labels
question: At a threshold your control has precision 0.18 and recall 0.89 on a base rate of 0.5%. What does precision 0.18 mean for customers?
options: 18% of fraud is caught
Of the orders you blocked, 82% were from good customers
18% of good customers are blocked
The model is wrong 18% of the time
explain: Precision is TP / (TP + FP). At 0.18, only 18% of blocked orders were fraud; the other 82% were honest customers. With rare fraud, even a small false positive rate creates this.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Adaptive adversaries: shadow mode, response and running the programme
question: A month after your 4-cards-per-device rule launched, its hits fell 90%, but fraud losses are unchanged and many devices now try exactly 3 cards. What does this indicate?
options: The rule solved the problem
Card networks changed their rules
A data pipeline bug
Attackers adapted to the threshold; losses, not rule hits, measure success
explain: Clustering just under a threshold with flat losses is classic adaptation. Combine the count with outcomes and amounts, avoid revealing exact thresholds, and track loss as the ground truth.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: When fsync lies or fails: drive caches and fsyncgate
question: A checkpointer's fsync of a data file returns EIO. Which response is safe on Linux?
options: Call fsync again until it returns 0, then continue
Crash deliberately and replay the WAL from the last checkpoint
Close the file, reopen it and fsync the new descriptor
Ignore it: the next checkpoint will write the page again
explain: The failed pages may already be marked clean and dropped, so a retry can report success with the data lost, and a fresh descriptor may not see the old error at all. The WAL still holds every change since the last checkpoint, so redo can rebuild the pages.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: A real hunt with libFuzzer: harness, run log and the crash
question: In the run log, what does the line '#1045 NEW cov: 6 ... DE: "TLV1"' tell you?
options: The fuzzer crashed at execution 1045
The user supplied a dictionary file containing TLV1
Input number 1045 reached new coverage, built with a dictionary entry TLV1 that comparison tracing discovered
The corpus was minimised to 6 inputs
explain: NEW means new coverage and a new corpus entry; the DE field names the dictionary entry used. No dictionary file was supplied: trace-cmp observed the comparison against TLV1 and learned the token.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Crash triage: deduplicate, minimise, root-cause, fix
question: Two crash files both end in memcpy inside parse_tlv, but one is reached from load_config() and one from load_profile(). How should a stack-hash deduplicator with the top 3 frames treat them?
options: Always as one bug, because the faulting line is the same
As zero bugs, because memcpy is a library function
As two separate buckets, since frame 3 (the caller of parse_tlv) differs, even though they may be one root cause
It cannot hash them without source code
explain: Stack hashes include callers, so different paths into the same bug make different buckets. That is the over-counting Klees et al. measured. A human or a fix-based check (does one patch fix both?) merges them.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Protocol and stateful fuzzing, and the Broadcom Wi-Fi case
question: Why does AFLNet use the server's response codes as feedback, in addition to code coverage?
options: Response codes are faster to compute than coverage
They replace the need for seeds
They reveal which protocol state the server reached, so sequences reaching new states are kept even when coverage alone is ambiguous
They detect memory corruption
explain: Its README describes identifying server states from response codes and steering towards progressive regions of the state space. State feedback complements coverage: the same code can run in different states.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Writing the report and coordinating disclosure
question: Under Project Zero's Full 90 policy, a vendor ships a patch on day 47. When are the technical details published?
options: Day 47, with the patch
Day 77, 30 days after the patch
Day 90
Never, once a patch exists
explain: Full X means details are published on day X regardless of when the patch shipped, unless the vendor asks for earlier release. Day 47 to day 90 is the window for users to update.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Weighted edits and the noisy channel: why the likely word wins
question: Two candidates are each 1 edit from a typo. Candidate A is 50 times as frequent as B, but B's slip is 100 times as likely as A's according to the confusion matrices. Which one does the noisy channel pick?
options: A, because at equal edit distance the more frequent word always wins
Neither: equal edit distance means a tie that needs a random choice
A, because the prior always outweighs the channel
B, because its product P(x|w) x P(w) is twice A's
explain: Write A's slip probability as p. A scores p x 50f and B scores 100p x f, so B wins by a factor of 2. Frequency only decides alone when every slip is equally likely, which is the assumption a plain edit distance makes.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Levenshtein automata, SymSpell and fuzzy queries in production
question: A Levenshtein automaton for query `fuzzy` with k = 1 reaches a state where every entry of the DP row is 2 after reading `ja`. Why can it reject every term starting with `ja` without reading further?
options: Because terms starting with ja are rare
Because the row minimum never decreases as more characters are read, so the final distance will be at least 2
Because the automaton only accepts terms of exactly 5 characters
Because Lucene sets prefix_length to 2
explain: Each new cell is at least the minimum of the previous row (diagonal moves add 0 or 1, the others add 1), so a row whose minimum is 2 can only lead to distances of 2 or more. That dead state lets the engine skip the entire ja block of the sorted term dictionary.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
question: A quad's code is (0.30, 0.40, 0.90, 0.20). What is the code of the same four stars if the labels A and B had been swapped?
explain: Swapping A and B turns the frame 180 degrees about (0.5, 0.5), so every coordinate becomes 1 minus itself. Here the original has xC + xD = 1.2, which is more than 1, and the swapped one 0.8, so the canonical labeling is the swapped one (then C and D trade places to get xC <= xD).

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: From an accepted match to a WCS header, and the triangle alternative
question: Groth's triangle matcher discards matched triangle pairs whose log perimeter ratio is far from the average. Why does that remove false matches?
options: False matches have larger perimeters
All true matches share one magnification between the lists, so their log perimeter ratios cluster, while false matches scatter
The perimeter is not scale invariant
It removes triangles with clockwise orientation
explain: Between two lists there is a single scale factor. Every truly corresponding triangle shows the same perimeter ratio; coincidental shape matches come from unrelated triangles of any size, so their ratios spread out. The same idea appears in Astrometry.net's scale-range check.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
question: How many cells does H3 resolution 2 have in total?
explain: c(r) = 2 + 120 x 7^r, so c(2) = 2 + 120 x 49 = 5,882. 122 is resolution 0 and 842 is resolution 1. The 12 pentagons are included in the count.

courseTitle: GPU image operators: resize, warp, color convert and convolution
lessonTitle: Warp and affine: an inverse map plus a border rule
question: A 5-tap filter on the row 10, 40, 90, 160 needs index -1 while computing output 0. Which rule returns 40 there?
options: REPLICATE
WRAP
REFLECT
REFLECT101
explain: REFLECT101 mirrors without repeating the edge, so index -1 maps to index 1, whose value is 40. REPLICATE clamps to index 0 and gives 10, REFLECT repeats the edge so it also gives 10, and WRAP folds to index 3, or 160. Only REFLECT101 reaches past the edge pixel to a real neighbour.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
question: You call torch.cuda.empty_cache() while a 3 MiB tensor is alive in a 20 MiB segment. How much of that segment is returned to the driver?
options: All 20 MiB, because only 3 MiB is in use
17 MiB, the free part
None of it, because the segment is split around a live block
3 MiB, the live tensor is moved to the small pool
explain: The allocator can only cudaFree a whole segment, and only when no block in it is in use. A partly used segment keeps all of its memory reserved, including the free 17 MiB.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Fixed-size suballocation for the KV cache, and diagnosing OOMs
question: A training job OOMs. memory_allocated is 30 GB, memory_reserved is 39 GB on a 40 GB GPU, and memory_summary shows 8 GB of inactive split blocks. What should you try first?
options: Enable expandable_segments to avoid stranded slivers in fixed segments
Call empty_cache() before every step
Switch to a smaller block size for the KV cache
Lower garbage_collection_threshold to 0.1
explain: 8 GB free inside split segments is fragmentation, which empty_cache cannot release because those segments hold live tensors. Expandable segments target exactly that; max_split_size_mb is the documented fallback.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Shared memory banks and bank conflicts
question: All 32 threads of a warp read `s[7]` from a shared float array. How many passes does the access need?
options: 32, because every thread uses bank 7
16, because pairs of threads share a pass
1, because the word is broadcast
2, because reads of one bank are paired
explain: A bank conflict needs different addresses in the same bank. Here every thread asks for the same word, which the hardware broadcasts in a single pass.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: The SOL gap: ranking many kernels by what they can return
question: After rewriting a kernel it runs in 0.62 ms instead of 0.90 ms, but its Memory Throughput row fell from 48 percent to 41 percent. What do you conclude?
options: The rewrite is a regression: the kernel now uses the memory system less efficiently
The measurement must be wrong, since less time with the same work implies a higher percent of peak
The rewrite is a 1.45x win; a SOL row can fall when the work itself shrinks, and duration is the thing you validate against
Nothing can be concluded without re-running with cache control disabled
explain: If the rewrite removed traffic, for example by fusing a pass or improving reuse, the kernel moves fewer bytes in less time, and the percent of peak can fall while the duration improves. The triage guide says to validate every change against absolute kernel duration for exactly this reason. The percentages are for classification, not scoring.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
question: A block of 256 threads executes `if (threadIdx.x < 96) heavy(); else light();`. How many of its 8 warps diverge on this branch?
options: 0: 96 is a multiple of 32, so the split falls on a warp boundary
3: warps 0 to 2 run heavy()
8: any if statement makes every warp run both paths
1: only the warp containing thread 96
explain: Threads 0 to 95 are exactly warps 0, 1 and 2; threads 96 to 255 are warps 3 to 7. Every warp's 32 threads agree, so no warp has to run both paths. Divergence is a per-warp property, not a per-block one.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Why chunk retrieval cannot answer 'what are the main themes?'
question: Why does increasing k (retrieving more chunks) not solve global questions on a 1-million-token corpus?
options: Because embeddings cannot represent questions
Because LLMs cannot read more than 10 chunks
Because chunks overlap by 100 tokens
Because the retrieved set is still ranked by similarity to the question and bounded by the context window, so it is a biased sample, not the whole corpus
explain: Retrieval chooses what is similar to the question words, and the context window caps how much fits. For "main themes" the relevant evidence is everywhere, so any top-k set is a sample presented as if it were a global view.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: What GraphRAG costs and how its gains were measured
question: Your corpus doubles from 1M to 2M tokens with the same settings. Roughly what happens to extraction LLM calls?
options: They stay the same because the graph is reused
They roughly double, because extraction runs once per chunk
They grow quadratically with the number of entity pairs
They halve because chunks get larger
explain: Extraction is one prompt (plus gleaning) per chunk, so it scales linearly with the number of chunks. Summaries and reports depend on graph size, which also tends to grow.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Group-relative advantages: the baseline from sibling answers
question: A group of 4 answers gets rewards 1, 0, 1, 0. Using the population std, what is the advantage of each correct answer?
explain: Mean 0.5, population std 0.5, so (1 - 0.5) / 0.5 = +1.0. Wrong answers get -1.0.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Failure modes and fixes: dead groups, entropy collapse, length bias
question: Under the original GRPO normalization, two wrong answers have the same advantage -1, one with 100 tokens and one with 1,000. How does the per-token push-down compare?
options: Equal per token
The 1,000-token answer's tokens are pushed down 10 times more each
Wrong answers get no gradient in GRPO
The 1,000-token answer's tokens are pushed down 10 times less each
explain: Each output's token terms are divided by its length, so each token of the long answer gets one tenth of the weight. Long wrong answers are cheap, which can drive response length up. Token-level (DAPO) or constant (Dr. GRPO) normalization removes this.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: GTFS Realtime messages and decoding them in Python
question: A consumer receives FULL_DATASET feeds every 30 s. At 08:10 the feed has a TripUpdate for T1. At 08:10:30 it does not. What should the app show for T1?
options: No realtime information: fall back to the schedule and say so, or hide the prediction
Keep the 08:10 prediction until a new one arrives
Mark T1 as canceled
Assume T1 is now exactly on time
explain: Each FULL_DATASET message is the whole state. A dropped entity means there is no realtime information for it now. It is not a cancellation (that is an explicit CANCELED), and the reference warns that absence must not be read as on time.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Phone phreaking: when the voice line was also the control line
question: Why did a 2600 Hz tone from a caller fool the far switch?
options: The switch could not tell a caller's tone from another switch's control tone, because both arrived on the same voice path
The tone carried a password the switch accepted
The tone overloaded the switch's power supply
The local switch forwarded it as a data packet
explain: In-band signalling means the control language travels in the same audio band as voices. Nothing marked a tone as coming from a switch rather than a person, so the far switch obeyed it.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Code Red, Slammer and Blaster: worms faster than people
question: Why did Slammer spread roughly 250 times faster than Code Red?
options: It used a more severe vulnerability
It targeted more popular software
One UDP packet was enough to infect, so each machine sent packets as fast as its bandwidth allowed instead of waiting for TCP handshakes
It exploited weak passwords
explain: The paper explains Slammer's scanner was limited only by bandwidth because a single UDP packet carried the whole worm. TCP-based worms like Code Red spend time waiting for each connection to be set up.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Leaks: Snowden, the Shadow Brokers and keeping bugs secret
question: What does the 2017 VEP charter mainly govern?
options: Export controls on encryption software
How CVE numbers are assigned
Bug bounty payments to researchers
Whether the US government discloses a newly found vulnerability to the vendor or temporarily keeps it for intelligence and law enforcement use
explain: The charter describes balancing equities between dissemination to the vendor (so it gets patched) and temporary restriction for national security purposes, with annual review of restricted items. CVE numbering is run by the CVE Program.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: What the incidents changed: laws, institutions and safer defaults
question: Which kind of change protected the most people who never read a security bulletin?
options: Criminal convictions
New review boards
Safer defaults such as firewalls on by default, blocked script attachments and AutoRun turned off
Government attribution statements
explain: Convictions and boards matter, but defaults act on every machine automatically. Most home users never configured anything, so turning protections on by default reached them directly.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf record: sampling on overflow, and the skid problem
question: You sample cycles with `perf record -c 3000000` on a core running steadily at 3 GHz. The program uses 2 seconds of CPU time. About how many samples do you get?
explain: 2 s x 3 GHz = 6 billion cycles; one sample every 3 million cycles gives 2000 samples. The 4000 Hz default only applies with frequency mode, not with -c.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Constant-time comparison in C, measured on a real machine
question: Which change turns leaky_equal into a constant-time function without other changes?
options: Compile with -O3 so the loop runs faster
Replace the loop body with diff |= a[i] ^ b[i] and return diff == 0 after the loop
Add a random usleep() before returning
Compare from the last byte to the first instead
explain: Accumulating differences and deciding once after the loop removes the data-dependent early exit. Speed, reversed order and random sleeps all keep the dependency.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Spectre variant 2: injecting indirect branch targets
question: What does a retpoline rely on to prevent branch target injection?
options: It encrypts function pointers
It turns the indirect jump into a return whose prediction comes from the RSB entry it created itself, so the BTB is never consulted
It disables the branch predictor completely
It moves the branch target into the kernel
explain: The direct call plants a known RSB entry that leads to a harmless loop; the real target is taken from the stack only when the return resolves. Attacker training of the BTB is never used.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Rowhammer: flipping bits in memory you never wrote
question: A vendor says its DDR4 modules are 'Rowhammer-free because of TRR'. Which finding best tests that claim?
options: Kim et al. 2014 on DDR3
The Project Zero NaCl exploit
Cold boot attacks
TRRespass 2020, which flipped bits on 12 of 42 DDR4 modules by hammering many rows at once
explain: TRR tracks a limited number of aggressor rows. Many-sided hammering overwhelms the tracker, which TRRespass demonstrated on DDR4 modules sold with TRR.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: One request, two readers: why proxies and caches disagree
question: Why does connection reuse between a front end and a back end matter for request smuggling?
options: It makes TLS weaker on the back-end hop
Requests from different users travel on one byte stream, so a boundary error moves bytes from one user's request into another's
It doubles the number of requests the back end must handle
It stops the back end from reading headers
explain: Reuse is what puts several users' requests on the same stream. If each request had its own connection, leftover bytes would only ever affect the sender. TLS strength and request volume are unrelated to the boundary problem.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: HTTP/2 framing, and how downgrading brings desync back
question: A front end accepts HTTP/2 from clients and forwards HTTP/1.1 to the back end. It copies a client's transfer-encoding: chunked field into the rewritten request. What has gone wrong, by RFC 9113?
options: The request was malformed and should have been rejected, because Transfer-Encoding is a connection-specific field
Nothing, Transfer-Encoding is allowed in HTTP/2
The front end should have added a second Transfer-Encoding
The back end should switch to HTTP/3
explain: RFC 9113 forbids connection-specific fields such as Transfer-Encoding in HTTP/2 and says intermediaries MUST NOT forward malformed requests. Copying it creates the H2.TE variant.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: How HTTP caches decide: keys, freshness and Vary
question: A login response sets a session cookie with Set-Cookie and has Cache-Control: public, max-age=60. What does RFC 9111 say about Set-Cookie here?
options: Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching; this response could be stored and served to others
Set-Cookie always prevents caching
Set-Cookie makes the response private
Set-Cookie is stripped by every cache
explain: RFC 9111 section 7.3 says Set-Cookie does not inhibit caching. Some caches (nginx by default) refuse to store such responses, but you cannot rely on that; the origin must send no-store or private.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Detecting, responding, and practising safely
question: After fixing a web cache deception bug, why must you also revoke sessions or tokens?
options: Responses already stored or fetched may have exposed tokens; purging the cache does not invalidate copies an attacker already holds
Revoking makes the cache faster
RFC 9111 requires it
It is needed to enable HTTP/2
explain: The fix and the purge stop future exposure. Anything already read by an attacker, such as the access tokens in the ChatGPT case, stays valid until revoked.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
question: With the defaults, what does setting khugepaged/max_ptes_none to 0 trade away?
options: Faults no longer allocate huge pages
khugepaged will not collapse any range with even one unpopulated PTE, so sparse regions stay on 4 KiB pages but never bloat
Huge pages can no longer be swapped
khugepaged stops running
explain: max_ptes_none only governs collapse: at 0, a range must have all 512 PTEs populated. That removes collapse-induced bloat but fewer ranges become huge. Fault-time allocation is controlled by enabled and defrag, not this knob.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Measure recall yourself: MQAR and a tiny hybrid in code
question: Why does MQAR separate a recurrent model from attention more sharply than a test with a single query at the end?
options: A single query lets the model store little; with many queries at different times, every pair must stay retrievable at once
MQAR sequences are much longer, and recurrent models cannot run on long sequences
MQAR uses a larger vocabulary, which recurrent models cannot embed
With one query, attention cannot find the key
explain: With one question at the end, a recurrent model can in principle get by with whatever survived in its state. MQAR asks about every pair, in an order the model cannot predict, so all of them must be held simultaneously in the fixed state. Attention just looks each one up.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
question: A team must cut KV memory but keeps exact recall at 200K tokens. Which design is riskiest?
options: 1 full attention layer per 8 layers, Mamba-2 elsewhere
Mamba layers plus only 2048-token sliding window attention
Gated DeltaNet with a full attention layer every 4 layers
Parallel attention and SSM heads with global attention in the first, middle and last layers
explain: With only sliding window attention, no layer can look up a token 200K positions back exactly; that recall must survive inside the fixed Mamba state. The other three keep at least a few global attention layers that can read the whole KV cache.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: Convex combination: normalize, then weight with alpha
question: After min-max normalization, a query whose dense results all have cosine 0.80 to 0.81 gets dense scores spread from 0 to 1. What is the risk?
options: None; normalization makes scores comparable by design
Cosine scores become negative
Tiny, possibly meaningless cosine differences are stretched to the full range and can outweigh real BM25 differences
BM25 scores are rescaled to match the cosine range
explain: Min-max always maps the list's min to 0 and max to 1, regardless of how close they were. Our toy shows a milder version: a 0.11 cosine range became 0 to 1. Theoretical min-max (dividing from the known lower bound, -1 for cosine) keeps such near-ties close.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: When fusion hurts, and weighting per query
question: Your dense model was fine-tuned on your own query logs and beats BM25 by a wide margin in nDCG@10. Equal-weight RRF with BM25 lowers nDCG@10 slightly. What is the best reading?
options: RRF is broken; use score fusion
In domain, the strong dense ranking is diluted by equal votes from a weaker list; keep BM25 for recall or code queries but weight it down, and keep it only if labeled queries show a gain
BM25 must have a bug, because hybrid always helps
Increase the rank window so BM25 contributes more
explain: This is Chen et al.'s in-domain pattern: on MS MARCO, RRF raised recall@1000 but lowered MAP against the dense model alone. Fusion helps most when the sides are comparable and fail differently. Weighting or routing keeps BM25's value for identifiers without letting it outvote the stronger model on every query.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Latency, cost, and when HyDE hurts
question: Users of an internal tool type short product code names that the LLM has never seen. HyDE with N=8 is underperforming plain dense retrieval. What is the best first change?
options: Give the raw query far more weight, or skip HyDE for these queries: every sample shares the same misreading, so averaging cannot fix it
Raise N to 32 so the noise averages out
Raise the temperature for more diverse passages
Switch the encoder for the hypothetical passages only
explain: Unfamiliar names produce a shared bias, which more samples cannot remove (lesson 3), and N=8 even shrinks the query's weight to 1/9. Routing these queries to plain or lexical retrieval, or weighting the query up, addresses the cause. Switching encoders breaks the shared embedding space.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: The Purdue model: levels from field devices to the enterprise
question: Under NIST's Purdue guidance, how should business users get production numbers from the plant historian?
options: Connect directly to the Level 3 historian from Level 4
Email the operators
Query the PLCs directly so the data is fresher
Read a replica of the historian in the DMZ, which the plant pushes data to
explain: Data is handed over in the DMZ so no business system connects into the control network. A replica historian (pushed from inside, ideally one way) is the classic pattern; lesson 13 adds unidirectional gateways.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: How attacks on physical processes work
question: Which single check would have caught the attack earliest in the scenario?
options: Waiting for the HMI high-level alarm
A monthly review of historian trends
A monitoring rule on Modbus writes from hosts other than the HMI
Rebooting the HMI
explain: The write happened at minute 10 and produced a network event at once. The HMI alarm would never fire because the HMI showed replayed data, and monthly reviews are far too slow.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: IT/OT convergence: Colonial, Oldsmar, Unitronics, Volt Typhoon
question: What made the Unitronics compromises possible, according to CISA?
options: A zero-day in Modbus
Stolen certificates
Internet-facing PLCs with default or no passwords on default ports
Insider sabotage
explain: No advanced exploit was needed. Removing the devices from the internet and changing default passwords would have stopped this campaign; CISA's primary mitigations list exactly these.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: One login, many apps: identity providers, service providers and trust
question: A company moves 30 apps behind one IdP. Which statement is true?
options: MFA and offboarding now happen in one place, and that place becomes the most valuable account system to attack
The apps can now verify Ana's MFA themselves
Each app no longer needs a session of its own
Password phishing becomes impossible
explain: Centralising login concentrates both benefit and risk: one place to enforce MFA and remove access, and one key that every app trusts. Apps still keep their own sessions, and the IdP's own login page can still be phished unless MFA is phishing-resistant.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Validating a SAML response: every check, and the replay cache
question: An SP checks the signature, Issuer and time window, but not the Audience. Which attack does that allow?
options: A malicious or compromised SP that receives the user's assertions can replay them to this SP and log in as those users
None, the signature is enough
XML signature wrapping
Login CSRF only
explain: Every SP that federates with the same IdP receives genuine, signed assertions about its users. Without the Audience check, any of them (or anyone who breaches one) can present those assertions here. It is the SAML twin of accepting a JWT with someone else's aud.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Setting up trust: metadata, signing certificates and key rollover
question: An SP's library verifies a SAML signature using the certificate in the response's own KeyInfo element. What can an attacker do?
options: Sign an assertion with any key of their own and include its certificate, so verification succeeds
Nothing, the certificate proves who signed
Only replay old assertions
Only cause a denial of service
explain: A certificate in the message proves only that the message was signed with the key in that certificate. The trust decision must come from the IdP's metadata the SP stored in advance; Somorovsky's paper lists untrusted KeyInfo keys among the bugs it found.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: IdP compromise and Golden SAML: forging the whole federation
question: An attacker holds a stolen AD FS token-signing key. The security team resets every user's password and re-enrols MFA. What is the effect on forged assertions?
options: None: forged assertions never involve passwords or MFA, so they keep working until the key is replaced everywhere it is trusted
They stop working, because passwords changed
They work only for administrators
They work only until the next AD FS reboot
explain: Reiner's write-up and MITRE both make this point: forging bypasses authentication entirely. Only replacing the signing key (twice, lesson 14) and removing the attacker's access stop it.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Who has access, why, and who said so: identity governance
question: Which of these is an identity governance question rather than an authentication or per-request authorization question?
options: Did this login present a valid passkey for ana@corp.example?
Should Ana, who moved from finance to sales in March, still hold the payments role?
May the request GET /invoices/1002 return invoice 1002 to user 7?
Has this session cookie expired?
explain: Governance asks whether an entitlement should exist at all, over time. The passkey check and cookie expiry are authentication and session questions; the invoice check is the per-request authorization decision from the access control course.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Role mining and role engineering: from a pile of grants to roles
question: Why do role-mining tools use heuristics such as greedy selection instead of always finding the minimal set of roles?
options: Because minimal role sets are always insecure
Because Vaidya, Atluri and Guo showed the role mining problem is NP-complete, so exact solutions do not scale
Because RBAC forbids more than ten roles
Because the user-permission matrix is secret
explain: The 2007 SACMAT paper proved RMP NP-complete by reduction from the set basis problem. Large real matrices therefore need approximate methods.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Bastions, jump hosts and session brokering
question: Why is `ssh -J bastion db1` safer than logging in to the bastion and then running `ssh -A` onward?
options: Because -J uses a stronger cipher
Because with -J the end-to-end session runs from the laptop and keys stay there, while -A lets anyone who controls the bastion use the forwarded agent's keys
Because -J disables logging on the bastion
Because -A only works with passwords
explain: The ssh manual says agent forwarding lets users who can bypass file permissions on the remote host use the local agent, and names a jump host (-J) as the safer alternative.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Measuring identity hygiene, detecting abuse, and running the programme
question: A dashboard shows a median time to deprovision of 5 hours. Why is that not enough to call leaver handling healthy?
options: Because medians are always wrong
Because the median hides the tail: a few leavers keeping access for days, often through applications without connectors, is where incidents like Cash App's come from
Because 5 hours is longer than NIST allows
Because time to deprovision should be measured in days
explain: In the sample, the median is 5 hours but 4 of 12 leavers kept access for over a day and one for 400 hours. Report high percentiles and the maximum, and fix the systems that cause the tail.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Differencing and picking a threshold with Otsu's method
question: If every pixel value in D were doubled (D' = 2D), how would Otsu's threshold and mask change?
options: The threshold doubles and the mask stays the same
The threshold stays the same and the mask doubles in size
Both stay the same
The threshold quadruples because variance scales with the square
explain: Scaling all values by 2 multiplies every class mean by 2 and every variance by 4, so the ranking of splits is unchanged: the same pixels are separated, at a threshold value twice as large. The variance scales by 4, but the threshold is a pixel value, not a variance.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Preparation: plan, people, contacts, retainers and logs
question: Why should the incident bridge for a suspected intrusion run on an out-of-band channel?
options: Because corporate chat is too slow
Because regulators require it
Because the usual channels may be down, and an intruder with access may be reading them
Because out-of-band channels are encrypted and corporate ones are not
explain: Both reasons appear in real cases: the HSE lost email and phones, and CISA warned SolarWinds victims that the actor may watch defenders' activity, so remediation plans should be shared out of band.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Hashing evidence and keeping a chain of custody
question: Six months later, a lawyer asks you to prove the memory image used in your report is the one taken from WKS-07. What answers that?
options: The custody log: who acquired it and when, each transfer, and the SHA-256 recorded at acquisition matching the image's hash today
The file name contains WKS-07
The file's modification date
Your memory of the day
explain: Names and dates are easy to change. A hash recorded at acquisition, matched today, plus an unbroken record of who held it, is the standard RFC 3227 and NIST describe.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Memory forensics: processes, connections and injected code
question: A process appears in windows.psscan output but not in windows.pslist. What is the right next step?
options: Investigate it: it may have exited, or it may have been unlinked from the active list to hide. Check its parent, times and command line
Ignore it; psscan produces false positives
Delete it from memory
Re-acquire memory because the image is corrupt
explain: psscan finds process structures anywhere in the image, including exited or hidden ones. A mismatch is not proof of malice, but it is exactly the kind of difference worth explaining.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Communication: staff, customers, regulators and the legal clocks
question: A listed US company determines on a Thursday that an incident is material. With no holidays, what is the latest day to file the Item 1.05 Form 8-K?
options: The following Monday
The following Tuesday
The following Wednesday
Exactly 96 hours later, on Monday
explain: The rule counts four business days after the determination: Friday, Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday. Weekends are skipped, so it is not a 96-hour calendar clock like GDPR's 72 hours.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: SQL from zero: tables, queries, quotes and comments
question: What does `SELECT 'O''Brien';` return?
options: A syntax error, because there are three quotes
The text O'Brien
The text O''Brien with two quotes
The text O, then a second statement Brien
explain: Inside a string literal, two single quotes in a row stand for one quote character. The literal is 'O''Brien' and its value is O'Brien. A lone quote in the same place would end the literal instead.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: Why escaping is fragile
question: A developer escapes quotes in every input before building SQL. Which query is still injectable?
options: SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '<escaped input>'
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = <escaped input>
Neither; escaping quotes fixes SQL injection
Both, because escaping never works
explain: In the numeric query the input is not inside quotes, so there is nothing for quote escaping to do, and input such as 5 OR 1=1 changes the logic. The string query is protected by correct escaping in this dialect, which is exactly the fragile kind of guarantee to avoid.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: NoSQL injection: when a value turns into an operator
question: Why does a JSON body `{"password": {"$ne": ""}}` bypass a MongoDB login that uses `findOne({username, password})`?
options: MongoDB parses the password string as SQL
The value is an object, so MongoDB treats $ne as an operator and matches any non-empty password
The $ character disables authentication
MongoDB ignores fields it does not recognise
explain: No string was parsed. JSON allowed the client to send an object where the code expected a string, and objects with $ keys are operators in MongoDB queries.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: LDAP, XPath, header and log injection
question: An app checks logins with the LDAP filter `(&(uid=` + user + `)(userPassword=` + pw + `))`. Which defence does OWASP list first?
options: Parameterised LDAP queries, which every LDAP library provides
Escaping each value with an LDAP encoding function for the correct context (search filter or distinguished name)
Removing the letter u from input
Using HTTPS between the browser and the app
explain: LDAP APIs generally lack parameterised queries, so OWASP's first defence is escaping each variable with the correct library encoder: RFC 4515 rules for filters and RFC 4514 rules for distinguished names. Least privilege and allowlist validation come next.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
question: A hand-written submit path does: `*sq_tail = tail + 1;` then fills `sqe->fd`, `sqe->addr` and `sqe->len`, then calls `io_uring_enter`. What is wrong?
options: Nothing, since io_uring_enter is what actually submits
The tail must be decremented, not incremented
The kernel may read the SQE as soon as the tail moves (an SQPOLL thread can do so at any moment), so it can see stale fields; fill first, then release-store the tail
user_data must be set before fd
explain: The tail is the publication point. Once it moves, the SQE belongs to the kernel, and with SQPOLL a kernel thread may consume it without waiting for any system call. Always fill the SQE completely and then advance the tail with release semantics.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Threat modelling a device: who can reach it, and how
question: Which attacker position can reach a firmware signing key that all cameras trust?
options: Someone in Bluetooth range of one camera
Someone on the owner's Wi-Fi
Someone holding one camera, if the design is correct
An intruder in the maker's build and signing systems
explain: In a correct design the signing key never leaves the maker (ideally it sits in a hardware security module); cameras hold only a fingerprint of the public key. So the supply-chain position, the maker's own build and signing systems, is the one that can reach it. Radio, LAN and physical attackers can reach only what is on a unit.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Secure boot: a chain of trust that starts in ROM
question: Why does the ROM compare the hash of the image's public key with OTP, instead of storing the whole public key in OTP?
options: Hashes are more secure than keys
The ROM cannot read OTP
OTP space is small: a 32-byte fingerprint pins a much larger key (an RSA-3072 key is hundreds of bytes)
So that anyone can change the key later
explain: OTP is tiny (8 kB on the RP2350) and costly per bit. A SHA-256 fingerprint fixes exactly one key, as securely as storing it, in 32 bytes. ESP32 stores the digest of its RSA-3072 key the same way. It does not make the key changeable; that is the point of OTP.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Ripple20: one TCP/IP stack inside hundreds of products
question: A hospital runs infusion pumps from a vendor that has not yet shipped a Ripple20 fix. Which response matches CERT/CC's guidance?
options: Block IP-in-IP tunnelling and unneeded fragments at the network edge of the pumps' segment, monitor with the published IDS rules, and press the vendor for the update
Wait for the update and change nothing
Disable the pumps' network entirely forever
Replace the hospital's firewall with a newer model
explain: CERT/CC lists filtering of tunnelling, fragments and malformed traffic plus detection rules as interim measures while the vendor's patch is pending. Doing nothing leaves the risk; permanently disconnecting may stop clinical workflows; a new firewall without the specific rules changes nothing.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Medical devices: FDA section 524B, pacemakers and insulin pumps
question: A toy pump adds a MAC to each command frame but no counter or nonce. Which attack still works?
options: Changing the dose in a recorded frame
Sending a command without the key
None
Replaying a recorded frame unchanged
explain: A MAC detects changes and forgery, so altering the dose or sending without the key both fail. But a recorded frame is unchanged, so its MAC still verifies: without a counter, nonce or timestamp the pump cannot tell new from old. That is why the FDA lists anti-replay separately.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Prototype pollution: one request changes every object
question: Why does pollution of a Node.js server's Object.prototype affect users other than the attacker?
options: Because the polluted value is written into each user's session cookie
Because Object.prototype is shared by ordinary objects across the whole process, and the process serves every user until it restarts
Because Node.js copies prototypes to every worker thread on each request
It does not: each request gets a fresh Object.prototype
explain: All requests to one Node.js process share the same heap and the same built-in prototypes (lesson 1). A property added to Object.prototype by one request is inherited by objects created for every later request, until the process exits.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Fixing ReDoS: rewrite, bound, change engines, cap the input
question: A search endpoint does `new RegExp(req.query.q).test(title)` for each title. Which change removes the ReDoS risk while keeping plain-text search?
options: Escape the user's text so it matches literally, or use title.includes(q), and cap q's length
Wrap the call in try/catch
Add the g flag to the regex
Move the code into an async function
explain: The user controls the pattern itself, so they can write a catastrophic one. Literal matching removes the pattern language entirely and the cap bounds the cost. try/catch does not stop a slow match (it never throws), flags do not change backtracking, and async functions still run on the Event Loop.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: npm inside the process: one realm, full privileges, a seat belt
question: A team enables `node --permission --allow-fs-read=/app` and concludes that a malicious npm dependency can no longer read `/etc` or start processes. What does the Node.js documentation say about that conclusion?
options: It is correct: the permission model is a complete sandbox
It is wrong only on Windows
It is correct as long as --permission-audit is also set
It is wrong: the permission model is a seat belt for trusted code; malicious code can bypass it, so it limits mistakes and raises noise rather than containing an attacker
explain: The permissions page says the feature does not protect against malicious code and that such code can bypass it. Audit mode makes enforcement weaker, not stronger. Containment needs OS-level boundaries.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: Hardening Electron: preload, IPC, navigation and fuses
question: A preload script exposes `runCommand: (name, args) => ipcRenderer.invoke('run', name, args)` and the main handler runs whatever it receives. What is the best redesign?
options: Expose specific functions such as exportPdf(docId), and in the main handler check senderFrame.origin and validate docId before running a fixed program
Keep it but obfuscate the channel name
Move the same handler into the renderer
Turn off contextIsolation so the page can call Node.js directly instead
explain: The bridge should expose actions, not a general command runner, and the main process must verify both the sender and the arguments. Obfuscation is not access control, renderers should not run commands, and turning off isolation removes a wall rather than adding one.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: tcmalloc: rseq per-CPU caches, spans and Temeraire
question: Why can't tcmalloc's per-CPU pop just be an ordinary load and store of `current` without rseq?
options: It could; per-CPU data is never shared
Two threads can run on the same CPU in turn, and a preemption between the read and the store would let both pop the same object
x86 does not allow stores to per-CPU memory
The kernel zeroes per-CPU memory on every context switch
explain: A CPU is shared over time by many threads. Without rseq, T1 could read current, be preempted, T2 could pop the same slot and commit, and T1 would then return a duplicate. rseq turns preemption into a restart so the read-modify-write behaves atomically for that CPU without a lock or atomic instruction.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Checking linearizability: searching for a legal order
question: Your Knossos check runs out of memory on a 20-minute register test. Which change helps most without weakening what the test can detect?
options: Split the workload across many independent keys with a bounded number of operations per key
Lower the number of nemesis faults to zero
Record every timeout, including writes, as fail
Remove all reads so only writes are checked
explain: Independent keys bound concurrency and length per checked history, which is what drives the search cost. Removing faults removes the bugs you were looking for, recording write timeouts as fail creates false alarms, and without reads there is nothing to contradict.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
question: Why does the Triton matmul tutorial ship 16 hand-written configs instead of the full grid?
options: Because Triton rejects more than 16 configs per kernel
Because the compiler derives the remaining configs automatically
Because a curated list is a cheap prior: it costs 16 benchmarks per new shape instead of thousands
Because configs outside the list are numerically incorrect
explain: The list is a hand-pruned subset chosen to cover the useful corners of the space. It trades the chance of finding the true optimum for a tuning cost that is affordable every time a new shape appears. Nothing in Triton limits the list length, and omitted configs are correct, just unmeasured.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
question: A design spends 100 cycles per packet allocating and initializing a generic packet struct. At 3.0 GHz, can one core forward 10 Gbit/s of minimum-size frames?
options: Yes, 100 cycles is well under the budget
Yes, as long as the copies are removed
No: the budget is about 200 cycles, and allocation alone takes half, leaving too little for receive, lookup and transmit
It depends only on the link's MTU (maximum transmission unit, the largest payload one frame may carry)
explain: The budget is 3.0 GHz x 67.2 ns, about 202 cycles. ixy measured DPDK's entire forwarding path at 61 cycles; a 100 cycle metadata step alone eats half of the line-rate budget before any real work.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Worked example: how SPDK reaches 10 million IOPS on one thread
question: Why does SPDK complete I/O by polling instead of waiting for interrupts?
options: NVMe drives cannot generate interrupts
With an I/O finishing every microsecond or less, taking an interrupt (stop, switch stacks, pollute the cache) costs too much, and routing interrupts to a user process is impractical
Polling uses less power
Interrupts are only available to the kernel's io_uring
explain: SPDK's docs give both reasons: interrupts into user space are not feasible for most hardware designs, and interrupt handling adds jitter and forced context switches. When completions arrive constantly, checking CQ memory is cheaper.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Driver signing: from cross-signing to Microsoft's portal
question: Microsoft attestation-signs a driver. What does that signature promise?
options: That Microsoft tested the driver for security bugs
That the driver passed the Hardware Lab Kit
That Windows trusts the publisher's identity and the file is unchanged, with no assurance about how the code behaves
That the driver is compatible with memory integrity
explain: Microsoft says attestation means Windows trusts the driver, but because it was not HLK-tested there are no assurances about compatibility or functionality. A signature binds a file to a vetted identity; it is not a code review.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Case files: BlackByte and Lazarus bring their own drivers
question: Dell released fixed versions of its driver in May 2021. Why could Lazarus still abuse CVE-2021-21551 that autumn on a machine that may never have run Dell software?
options: Because the fix was not signed
Because Dell's fix only applied to Windows 7
Because the attackers brought the old, validly signed vulnerable driver themselves, and nothing on the machine denied that file
Because CISA had not yet listed the CVE
explain: BYOVD does not depend on the victim having the vulnerable software installed. The attacker drops the old file. A patch changes the vendor's software on machines that run it; a deny rule is needed to stop the old file loading anywhere.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: VBS and memory integrity: taking code checks out of the kernel
question: With memory integrity on, an attacker uses a vulnerable driver's write IOCTL to copy code into a kernel pool buffer and then tries to run it. What stops them?
options: The driver's signature check
PatchGuard
Nothing: HVCI only protects user mode
The hypervisor refuses to make the page executable, because execute rights come only from VTL1 after a code integrity check
explain: Under memory integrity, kernel pages become executable only after passing code integrity checks in VTL1, and executable pages are never writable. Writing code into data memory does not make it runnable.

courseTitle: Windows kernel and driver security: BYOVD and kernel hardening
lessonTitle: Responding to a BYOVD alert, and the cost of kernel code
question: Which containment step is most reliable when the alert says the EDR sensor on the host stopped reporting after a suspicious driver load?
options: Ask the EDR agent on the host to isolate it
Run a full antivirus scan on the host
Wait for the sensor to come back
Isolate the host with network controls outside it, such as the switch port or firewall, and disable the admin account used
explain: If a BYOVD driver blinded the sensor, commands sent through that sensor may not work or may not be honest. Controls outside the host do not depend on its integrity, and disabling the compromised admin account cuts the attacker's access elsewhere.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Limits of fusion and how compilers decide
question: A fused kernel for a long row-wise reduction starts spilling registers and runs slower than two unfused kernels. Which fix matches what FlashAttention and Triton tutorials do?
options: Tile the reduction so each block of the row fits on chip, carrying running statistics between tiles
Fuse even more ops into the kernel
Switch to FP64 to get more registers
Disable the GPU's L2 cache
explain: Fusion is bounded by on-chip capacity. Tiling with running statistics (as in FlashAttention's online softmax) keeps the working set small while still avoiding HBM round trips for intermediates.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: A patient and consistent teacher: the recipe that makes KD work
question: Two runs differ only in schedule: 30 epochs and 9,600 epochs. Following Beyer et al.'s ImageNet table, which setup should win each run?
options: Function matching wins both; mixup always helps
Consistent teaching wins the short run; function matching wins the long run
The fixed teacher wins the short run, because caching is cheaper per step
All three tie at 9,600 epochs because every student eventually matches the teacher
explain: At 30 epochs consistent teaching leads (74.95% vs 73.89% for function matching). At 9,600 epochs function matching is best (82.31%), consistent teaching close behind (81.76%), and the fixed teacher has overfit (76.95%). Mixup only pays off when there is time to fit the harder inputs.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: An LLM distillation pipeline: logits, tokenizers, traces, compute
question: Your teacher uses a 150k-entry tokenizer and your student a 32k one, but you do have the teacher's full logits. Which option gives a logit-level signal at all?
options: Token-level forward KL after truncating the teacher to 32k entries
Token-level reverse KL, which does not need a shared vocabulary
On-policy GKD with beta = 0.5
ULD: sort both distributions at each position, pad, and penalize the absolute differences
explain: Every KL or JSD variant compares probabilities of the same token, which needs a shared vocabulary; truncating to 32k entries does not make the ids mean the same strings. ULD compares sorted probability vectors, so it only transfers the shape of the distribution, but it works across tokenizers. Seq-KD on generated text is the other option.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sharing keys and values across heads: MQA and GQA
question: You serve the released Llama 3 8B checkpoint and may not pretrain or uptrain it. Which of these architectural levers can you still apply?
options: Cross-Layer Attention with sharing factor 2
Switching to MLA with a 512-number latent
Palu's low-rank projection of the K and V weights
Dropping to one KV head (MQA)
explain: Palu decomposes the trained K and V projection matrices with SVD, picks ranks from a small calibration set and needs no fine-tuning. CLA, MLA and MQA change what the attention layer computes, so the model must be trained or uptrained with them.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
question: Your server runs an unmodified FlashAttention kernel for both prefill and decode, and you can afford one small extra computation right after prefill. Which method can you deploy without touching the kernels?
options: H2O, because its scores are a by-product of decoding
Both, since FlashAttention returns attention weights on request
SnapKV, because it scores the prompt once from a small observation window
Neither, since every eviction method needs the full attention matrix
explain: SnapKV only needs the observation window's attention over the prompt, a window x prompt block you can compute in a separate small pass once, after which the decode kernel reads an ordinary (shorter) cache. H2O needs per-key attention every decode step, which FlashAttention never materializes.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
question: A server runs Llama 3 8B with 40 GB of HBM free for KV and serves 200 users who each come back every few minutes with a growing 8K-token chat history. Without offloading, what happens on most return visits?
options: Prefix caching hits, because vLLM never evicts blocks that another request might reuse
The history was evicted from HBM (only about 37 such histories fit), so prefill recomputes it
The attention kernel reads the history directly from CPU memory over PCIe
The request is rejected until enough HBM is freed
explain: 200 histories of 1 GiB each cannot fit in 40 GB; only about 37 can. Free blocks are evicted when space is needed, so most returning users miss and pay a full prefill. Offloading to a 512 GB DRAM tier would keep all 200 histories.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, capacity and reuse
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
question: In SGLang HiCache with the best_effort prefetch policy, a 4,000-token L3 hit is only half fetched when the GPU becomes free. What happens?
options: The fetched part is used with the local hits and the rest is computed by prefill
The request waits until all 4,000 tokens arrive
The partial prefetch is discarded and everything is recomputed
The request is moved to another instance that has the data in L2
explain: best_effort terminates prefetching as soon as the GPU can run prefill. The data already fetched is used together with the local data, and the remaining tokens are prefilled. wait_complete would have waited for all of it.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
question: In the three-node run, which pair of events is related by happened-before?
options: a3 and c2, because a3 is on A, which started the chain
c1 and c2, because they are on the same node and c1 comes first
a3 and b2, because both happen late in the run
c1 and a2, because c1 is drawn to the left of a2
explain: c1 and c2 are on the same process with c1 first, so rule 1 gives c1 happened before c2. There is no message path from a3 to anything, so a3 is concurrent with b2 and c2. c1 and a2 are concurrent too: being drawn further left is not causality.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
question: An operator lowers CockroachDB's max offset to 250 ms. Using the 80% rule, at what offset from at least half of the other nodes will a node shut itself down?
options: 250 ms
125 ms
200 ms
400 ms
explain: 0.8 x 250 = 200 ms. 400 ms is the threshold for the 500 ms default. A smaller max offset shrinks uncertainty windows (fewer restarts) but makes spurious self-termination more likely when clocks or networks wobble.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
question: A 200-token passage is stored with ColBERTv2 at 2 bits per dimension, 128 dimensions. How many bytes does it take, ignoring the inverted list?
options: 7,200 bytes
6,400 bytes
51,200 bytes
800 bytes
explain: Each vector is a 4-byte centroid id plus 128 x 2 bits = 32 bytes of residual, 36 bytes total. 200 x 36 = 7,200. 6,400 forgets the centroid id, 51,200 is float16 (200 x 128 x 2), and 800 counts only the ids.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
question: In latent mode at position t (between <bot> and <eot>), what is the input vector?
options: The embedding of the argmax token of softmax(W h at t-1)
A learned <pause> embedding that is the same at every latent position
